analysis.one_liner: Requires hospitals, nursing homes, and social service employers to adopt workplace violence prevention plans, training, and incident reporting.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require hospitals, nursing homes, and social service employers to adopt workplace violence prevention plans, has been stuck in three House committees since its April 2025 introduction, with no committee action or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Health care and social service workers face some of the highest rates of workplace violence of any occupation — assaults from patients, clients, and visitors. This bill directs the Labor Department to write a binding federal safety standard requiring employers in these sectors to assess violence risks, maintain a written prevention plan, investigate incidents, keep records, train staff, and protect workers who report violence. Hospitals and nursing homes would have to comply to keep participating in Medicare. The bill is currently sitting in three House committees with no scheduled action.
analysis.who_benefits: Health care and social service workers — nurses, aides, nursing home staff, home health workers, emergency responders, and social workers — would get enforceable federal protections: required prevention plans, risk assessments, incident investigations, annual training, recordkeeping, and an anti-retaliation guarantee. Patients and clients also benefit from safer facilities. The workers most exposed are disproportionately women and low-wage staff in long-term care and home care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Health care and social service workers

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered employers to develop a written workplace violence prevention plan tailored to each facility, developed with the participation of direct-care employees and their representatives [S2, S3].
Requires prompt investigation of every violent incident and correction of the hazards that caused it, plus annual evaluations of whether the plan is working [S3].
Requires annual training for workers, including hazard-recognition training for supervisors so they do not assign staff to predictably dangerous situations [S3].

Requires employers to keep a violent incident log and records for at least five years, available to employees and their representatives, and to submit annual summaries to the Labor Department, which reports to Congress [S3].
Prohibits employers from retaliating against workers who report violent incidents, threats, or concerns [S3].
Makes compliance with the standard a condition of Medicare participation for hospitals and skilled nursing facilities not otherwise covered by OSHA, giving the rule real teeth [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — hospitals, nursing homes, residential treatment and group home operators, home health agencies, and similar facilities — would pay for prevention plans, training, security and engineering controls (alarms, access controls, camera systems), and incident recordkeeping, and would face OSHA enforcement for failures. Some of that cost could be passed to patients, insurers, and government health programs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Hospitals, nursing homes, and care providers

drawbacks.text: The bill tells the Labor Department to issue its rule on an expedited track, skipping some of the usual rulemaking requirements, including normal review under Executive Order 12866 and the Paperwork Reduction Act, with only a 30-day public comment window on the interim standard [S3].

Compliance costs fall on employers: written prevention plans tailored to each facility, annual in-person training, engineering controls such as alarm systems and secured items, and detailed violent incident logs maintained for five years [S3]. Smaller providers such as group homes and community clinics may find these requirements harder to absorb than large hospital systems.

The standard covers a very broad range of settings, including field work like home health care and even emergency responders' services, which could make implementation complicated and uneven across sectors.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is a concrete safety rule for workers in one of the most violence-exposed occupations, using prevention methods (risk assessment, training, incident logs, anti-retaliation) that are well established in state laws and OSHA guidance. The costs are compliance paperwork and possible capital spending for hospitals, nursing homes, and social service agencies, and the bill's fast-track process limits the usual public review. On balance the safety gains for a large, frequently assaulted workforce appear to outweigh the compliance costs, though the regulatory burden on small providers deserves attention.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to three House committees in April 2025, and none of them has taken it up since.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 1, 2025 and referred to the House Education and Workforce, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means committees [S5].
No further action appears in the record: no hearings, markup, committee vote, or floor action has occurred [S5].
The bill has 134 cosponsors, including 5 Republicans, but that support has not translated into committee movement [S1, S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: For now, employers in the health care and social service sectors are better off: no federal violence-prevention standard has been imposed, and the status quo of voluntary OSHA guidelines continues.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health care and social service employers

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship is overwhelmingly Democratic — 129 of 134 cosponsors — with a small bipartisan element of 5 Republicans, including original cosponsors Bacon and Fitzpatrick [S4].

industries.note: They would bear new compliance costs — prevention plans, training, engineering controls, incident logs — and Medicare participation would be conditioned on following the standard. Their interest in avoiding these requirements runs against the safety interests of their workers and patients.

industries.industry: Home health, hospice, and social service agencies
industries.note: Covered services extend to field work like home health care and home-based social work, requiring plans, training, and reporting even outside facility walls.

Emergency services and transport, including services by firefighters and emergency responders, are covered services, adding training and reporting obligations but also formal safety protections for responders.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action more than a year into the Congress and a referral spread across three committees, the bill's odds are poor; most bills parked at this stage die when the Congress ends. Its strongest lever is that a similar version passed the House in the previous Congress, but in a divided Congress with no committee activity, a floor vote is unlikely without a scheduling push from leadership.
